paragraphs: When some classes have many more examples than others, minimizing average training error can favor the common classes. Two ways to compensate are to give different classes different loss weights or to adjust their prediction scores, called logits. Both change what training emphasizes, but existing theory has not fully explained their observed behavior.

This paper develops a shared analysis of these approaches using a technique called data-dependent contraction. The technique accounts for how modified losses affect individual classes, rather than treating their effects only in aggregate. It supports a more detailed generalization bound: a theoretical description of how learning from the available examples relates to performance beyond those examples.

The authors also turn their theoretical insights into a learning algorithm. Benchmark experiments support the analysis and demonstrate the method’s effectiveness. The contribution connects two common practical interventions through one class-sensitive framework, helping explain their behavior and providing a principled basis for designing a loss for imbalanced data.
neurips-2023-a-unified-generalization-an.tldr: A class-sensitive generalization analysis unifies loss re-weighting and logit adjustment and motivates an effective algorithm for imbalanced learning.

paragraphs: Assigning semantic labels to LiDAR point clouds requires substantial annotation work because each scan contains many points. Annotator addresses this with active learning: the model selects which parts of a scan should receive labels. Its selection operates on voxels, small spatial cells that group nearby points.

The authors first examine common selection rules, including random sampling and rules based on prediction uncertainty. They then introduce voxel confusion degree, which uses local relationships and structure within the point cloud. An online selection strategy seeks informative, representative voxels within each scan, including when the data distribution changes.

Experiments cover active learning and two forms of active domain adaptation, across simulated-to-real and real-to-real transfers. In the SynLiDAR-to-SemanticKITTI task, labeling five voxels per scan reaches 87.8%, 88.5%, and 94.4% of fully supervised performance in the three respective settings. These are relative performance levels, illustrating how carefully selected local annotations can provide substantial value with a small labeling budget.
neurips-2023-annotator-a-generic-active-.tldr: Annotator selects informative LiDAR voxels for labeling and achieves strong segmentation results with very few annotated regions.

paragraphs: Continual learning studies how a model can acquire tasks sequentially while retaining earlier knowledge. This paper moves that question into abstract reasoning, including concepts such as counting, sorting, and arithmetic. These tasks offer a different setting from the image-based problems that dominate much continual-learning research.

CLeAR maps inputs into a shared space through a one-to-many mapping. This is intended to align tasks that differ in dimensionality while sharing semantic structure. The authors express the tasks as formal languages and organize their difficulty using the Chomsky hierarchy, allowing experiments both within a hierarchy level and across different levels.

Across experiments involving 15 tasks, CLeAR exhibits almost no forgetting. Learning later tasks also improves accuracy on earlier ones, an effect called backward transfer. Existing continual-learning methods developed for image classification perform poorly in these experiments. The findings show that a representation designed to align abstract tasks can support both retention and beneficial transfer in the studied algorithmic-reasoning setting.
neurips-2023-clear-continual-learning-on.tldr: CLeAR aligns sequential abstract-reasoning tasks in a shared space, achieving near-zero forgetting and beneficial backward transfer in its experiments.

paragraphs: An autonomous agent can benefit from reusable skills that organize behavior over different lengths of time. The challenge is deciding which skills are useful and how they should fit together. This paper derives that organization from a graph describing possible interactions between an agent and its environment.

The central procedure uses modularity maximization to reveal structure in the interaction graph at multiple levels. That structure produces a hierarchy in which longer-duration skills are built from shorter-duration ones. The method automatically determines each skill’s behavior, the circumstances in which it can be invoked, its termination conditions, and its dependencies on other skills.

This matters because the hierarchy supplies both reusable behaviors and a way to compose them, without requiring a person to design those components individually. Across a broad range of tested environments, the resulting hierarchies are described as intuitively meaningful and substantially improve learning performance. The evidence supports interaction-graph structure as a useful organizing principle for automatically constructing skills at several time scales.
neurips-2023-creating-multi-level-skill-.tldr: The method automatically builds multilevel skill hierarchies from interaction graphs and substantially improves agent learning in tested environments.

paragraphs: In synchronous distributed training, many workers compute parts of a training step, but the next step must wait until every worker finishes. This makes slow workers consequential even when most workers finish quickly. As the system grows, variability in computation time can limit the benefit of adding more workers.

DropCompute studies the setting where these delays arise from differences in compute time. The authors derive an analytical relationship between properties of those times and the resulting limits on scalability. They then use that relationship to design a decentralized method that reduces variation across workers and makes synchronous training more robust to stragglers.

The method can be integrated with All-Reduce, a widely used component of synchronous training systems. The authors validate their findings on large training tasks using 200 Gaudi accelerators. The central contribution is to connect a mathematical account of waiting-time bottlenecks with a practical way to reduce their impact while retaining a synchronous training approach.
neurips-2023-dropcompute-simple-and-more.tldr: DropCompute reduces variation in worker computation times to make synchronous distributed training more robust to stragglers.

paragraphs: Audio-visual source localization identifies which objects in a video frame are producing the accompanying sound. Learning only from audio-image correspondence can leave imprecise boundaries, false detections, and difficulty with small objects. The paper investigates how a small amount of positional annotation can help exploit a much larger collection of unlabeled pairs.

Dual Mean-Teacher uses two teacher-student structures to address confirmation bias, where a model reinforces its own incorrect predictions. Both teachers are initially trained with limited labeled data. Agreement between their predictions filters noisy samples, and intersections of their confidence maps provide pseudo-labels for further learning.

With positional annotations for only 3% of the data, the method reports CIoU scores of 90.4% on Flickr-SoundNet and 48.8% on VGG-Sound Source. The abstract reports improvements of 8.9% and 9.6%, respectively. Applying the framework to existing localization methods also consistently improves their performance, supporting the usefulness of teacher agreement for making unlabeled audio-visual examples more informative.
neurips-2023-dual-mean-teacher-an-unbias.tldr: Two cooperating teacher models produce cleaner pseudo-labels, improving audio-visual localization with only a small amount of positional annotation.

paragraphs: Adversarial training can improve resistance to deliberately perturbed inputs, yet that resistance may be much stronger on training examples than on unseen data. This discrepancy is the robust generalization gap. The paper investigates whether commonly used measures actually track that gap across varied experimental settings.

The measures include quantities based on margins, smoothness, and flatness. Rather than introducing another measure, the authors conduct a large empirical comparison to examine when and how existing measures capture robust generalization. Their main analysis covers more than 1,300 models trained on CIFAR-10 with adversarial perturbations constrained by the L-infinity norm.

They further evaluate more than 100 RobustBench models spanning CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet. This extends the investigation beyond the initial collection of trained models. The contribution is empirical evidence about the circumstances in which robustness measures are informative. Its relevance is diagnostic: understanding those relationships can help researchers assess robust overfitting and guide work toward defenses that generalize better.
neurips-2023-fantastic-robustness-measur.tldr: A large empirical study examines when margin, smoothness, and flatness measures meaningfully capture the robust generalization gap.

paragraphs: Meta-learning aims to help models adapt quickly to new tasks using little data. A practical complication is that tasks may come from several distinct sources, and a new task may come from a source absent during training. Treating all tasks as samples from one shared component overlooks both possibilities.

The proposed Hierarchical Gaussian Mixture based Task Generative Model represents task instances probabilistically. It learns task embeddings, fits a mixture distribution over tasks, and assigns density-based scores to new tasks. This provides one framework for modeling multiple task populations and detecting tasks that are unfamiliar relative to the learned distribution.

Training uses maximum likelihood estimation through an Expectation-Maximization algorithm, with the parameters learned end to end. The framework can work with different encoders and scales to large backbone networks. Benchmark experiments support its effectiveness for both classifying samples and detecting novel tasks, linking rapid adaptation with an explicit model of where tasks come from.
neurips-2023-hierarchical-gaussian-mixtu.tldr: HTGM models multiple task populations with a hierarchical Gaussian mixture to support classification and detection of unfamiliar tasks.

paragraphs: Describing an image edit precisely in words can be difficult, especially when the intended transformation is visually specific. ImageBrush instead takes a pair of images demonstrating a transformation and uses that pair as an instruction for editing another image. The task is to infer the operation from the example and transfer it to new content.

The method formulates this instruction-learning problem as diffusion-based inpainting. Its iterative generation process uses visual context to construct the edited result. A dedicated visual prompting encoder strengthens the model’s ability to extract the intended transformation from the demonstration, giving visual examples a direct role in controlling the edit.

Experiments show outputs that follow the transformations demonstrated by the example pairs. The model also generalizes across tasks including pose transfer, image translation, and video inpainting. These findings support visual demonstrations as a useful interface for image manipulation, particularly when expressing the desired operation comprehensively through language would be burdensome.
neurips-2023-imagebrush-learning-visual-.tldr: ImageBrush learns edits from visual transformation pairs and applies those instructions to new images through diffusion-based inpainting.

paragraphs: Permutation matrices encode one-to-one assignments and appear in matching problems in vision and robotics. Their explicit storage grows quadratically with problem size, making large instances expensive. This paper proposes representing them through two smaller matrices whose low-rank product is followed by a nonlinear transformation.

The authors use kissing number theory to infer the minimum rank needed for a permutation matrix of a given size under this representation. That rank can be much smaller than the assignment problem itself. The nonlinear step is a key part of the proposed construction, connecting compact factors to accurate representations of large permutations.

For a problem of size 20,000, the abstract gives a representation using 840,000 elements instead of 400 million. This illustrates the substantial memory reduction that makes otherwise infeasible instances manageable. Experiments cover linear assignment, quadratic assignment, and shape matching, demonstrating the representation’s applicability to several settings where models must predict large permutation matrices.
neurips-2023-kissing-to-find-a-match-eff.tldr: Low-rank factors followed by a nonlinearity compactly represent large permutation matrices, substantially reducing memory and computation.

paragraphs: Small language models can be easier to deploy, but knowledge-intensive reasoning places demands on how much information they can memorize. Simply fine-tuning them on answers or distilling a larger model may leave that bottleneck unresolved. This paper uses an analysis of memorization to motivate combining distilled reasoning with retrieved knowledge.

Knowledge-Augmented Reasoning Distillation, or KARD, trains small models to generate rationales obtained from larger language models while supplying information from an external knowledge base. A neural reranker selects documents relevant to generating those rationales. The approach therefore gives the learner both examples of reasoning and access to supporting knowledge.

Experiments show substantial improvements for small T5 and GPT models on MedQA-USMLE, StrategyQA, and OpenbookQA. On the first two benchmarks, a 250-million-parameter T5 model outperforms fine-tuned models with 3 billion parameters. These results support retrieval-augmented reasoning distillation as an effective way to improve smaller models on the studied knowledge-intensive tasks.
neurips-2023-knowledge-augmented-reasoni.tldr: KARD combines retrieved knowledge with distilled reasoning rationales to substantially improve small language models on knowledge-intensive benchmarks.

paragraphs: An interpretable representation separates information into dimensions that correspond to meaningful properties, such as musical pitch. Many methods achieve this by incorporating substantial knowledge about music. This paper asks whether a more general computational principle can produce low-dimensional factors that agree with human perception.

The proposed principle is physical symmetry, imposed as a consistency requirement on the latent representation. Specifically, the model describing how latent states evolve must be equivariant under selected group transformations. In plain terms, transforming a latent state and then predicting its evolution must agree with applying the corresponding transformation to the predicted evolution.

Using this constraint, the model learns a linear pitch factor from unlabeled monophonic music audio. The same approach learns three-dimensional Cartesian space from videos of a simple moving object without labels. It also yields counterfactual representation augmentation, a technique reported to improve sample efficiency. Together, these results demonstrate the usefulness of symmetry constraints in the studied music and vision settings.
neurips-2023-learning-interpretable-low-.tldr: Symmetry constraints on latent dynamics produce interpretable pitch and spatial representations from unlabeled data and improve sample efficiency.

paragraphs: A generalizable implicit neural representation uses a coordinate-based network to represent multiple data instances, adapting the network with latent codes. The paper identifies a weakness in existing adaptation methods: they struggle to associate those codes with specific local details, such as individual pixels or rays.

The proposed framework combines a transformer encoder with a decoder designed around locality. The encoder produces several latent tokens that capture local information. For each queried coordinate, cross-attention selects and combines the relevant tokens into a modulation vector. The decoder then uses modulation across multiple frequency bands to build its prediction progressively from coarse structure to fine detail.

These two mechanisms address different aspects of detail: token selection determines which spatial information matters, while frequency-based modulation controls the scales of information being decoded. The authors report substantial improvements over previous generalizable implicit representations. They also demonstrate that the learned local latent representations are useful for downstream tasks such as image generation.
neurips-2023-locality-aware-generalizabl.tldr: Coordinate-specific token selection and coarse-to-fine modulation improve the local detail captured by generalizable implicit neural representations.

paragraphs: This paper studies the optimization behavior of a softmax-attention model to clarify how training selects tokens. The model combines token values using attention weights controlled by trainable parameters. Its analysis connects that selection process to maximum-margin separation, where preferred choices are separated as strongly as possible from alternatives.

The authors prove that gradient descent on the attention parameter converges in direction to a solution separating locally optimal tokens from non-optimal ones. Token optimality is characterized through value embeddings and the geometry of the problem. A broader analysis of regularization paths also establishes margin-maximizing behavior when prediction heads are nonlinear.

When value and attention parameters are optimized together with logistic loss, the paper identifies conditions for their regularization paths to converge directionally to hard-margin support-vector-machine solutions. The attention solution depends on the support-vector geometry of the value solution. Numerical experiments support the theory, providing a precise account of token selection for the analyzed model and optimization settings.
neurips-2023-max-margin-token-selection-.tldr: The analysis links softmax-attention training to maximum-margin selection of locally optimal tokens, with conditional results for jointly trained parameters.

paragraphs: Recovering an entire causal graph can require more interventions than a particular question needs. Targeted causal discovery instead seeks only the relevant part of the structure. This paper studies two such problems, subset search and causal matching, with the goal of reducing how many interventions they require.

Its main tool is a Meek separator: a set of vertices whose intervention splits the remaining edges with unresolved directions into smaller connected components. The authors give an efficient algorithm for finding small separators. This decomposition supports divide-and-conquer strategies by breaking unresolved structure into pieces that can be handled separately.

Using this tool, the paper develops randomized algorithms with logarithmic approximation guarantees for both target problems. It reports the first known provable average-case guarantees for them. The contribution establishes a useful structural operation and demonstrates how it supports intervention-efficient discovery; its possible extension to other targeted causal problems is presented as a direction opened by the results.
neurips-2023-meek-separators-and-their-a.tldr: Meek separators divide unresolved causal structure into smaller pieces, enabling randomized approximation algorithms for two targeted discovery problems.

paragraphs: Causal representation learning seeks hidden causal variables and their relationships from observations that mix those variables together. This paper allows both the mixing function and the causal model to be nonparametric. Its learning signal consists of datasets generated under interventions whose targets are unknown.

For two causal variables, the authors prove that observational data and one perfect intervention per variable are sufficient for identifiability under a genericity condition. That condition excludes finely tuned relationships between observational and intervened distributions that could create spurious solutions. For any number of variables, a pair of distinct perfect intervention environments per variable provides a sufficient guarantee.

Recovery is only up to ambiguities that the authors show cannot be resolved from interventional data. Nevertheless, all equivalent solutions preserve the strengths of causal influences, supporting causal conclusions from new observations. The results establish when hidden causal structure can be recovered in this general setting while explicitly accounting for what the available intervention evidence cannot distinguish.
neurips-2023-nonparametric-identifiabili.tldr: The paper establishes sufficient intervention conditions for identifying nonparametric latent causal models up to unavoidable ambiguities.

paragraphs: Predicting a molecule’s mass spectrum can help identify metabolites. Existing approaches face a trade-off: explicit fragmentation can be computationally difficult and restrictive about rearrangements, while discretized spectrum vectors lose information and physical structure. This paper introduces a representation between those two approaches.

The method first encodes the molecular graph, then predicts a set of molecular subformulae. Each subformula specifies a predicted spectral peak, and a second model predicts its intensity. Because a formula records counts of atom types, the output can be treated as a collection of multisets rather than a fixed vector of spectrum bins.

To manage the many possible subformulae, decoding follows a prefix tree and proceeds one atom type at a time. Shared partial formulas organize the output possibilities into a structured decoding process. The authors report promising empirical results on spectrum-prediction tasks and present the construction as a general approach to ordered multiset decoding, extending its conceptual relevance beyond this particular output format.
neurips-2023-prefix-tree-decoding-for-pr.tldr: A prefix-tree decoder predicts molecular subformulae for spectral peaks, with a separate model estimating their intensities.

paragraphs: Behavior cloning learns to imitate demonstrations through supervised learning. This paper develops a theoretical framework for complex expert behavior using generative models, with low-level controllers stabilizing execution around demonstrations. Those controllers may be learned or already implicit in position-command control.

The main guarantee requires suitable low-level stability and a sufficiently expressive generative learner. Under those conditions, behavior cloning can match the per-time-step distributions of essentially arbitrary expert trajectories in an optimal transport cost. The analysis uses a policy property called total variation continuity. The authors show how data augmentation combined with augmentation noise during execution can ensure this property with little loss of accuracy.

For diffusion-based policies, the paper further proves closeness between imitator and expert trajectory distributions when the learner accurately estimates the noise-augmented expert policy’s score. Experiments validate the algorithmic recommendations. The work explains how stable low-level execution and expressive high-level imitation can jointly support distributional guarantees, while keeping the required stability and estimation conditions explicit.
neurips-2023-provable-guarantees-for-gen.tldr: Under stability and modeling conditions, generative behavior cloning receives distributional guarantees strengthened by adding augmentation noise during execution.

paragraphs: Multi-task learning often combines task losses into a weighted sum, a procedure called linear scalarization. Changing those weights is a natural way to seek different compromises between tasks. This paper asks whether that procedure can reach every Pareto-optimal compromise, where improving one task would require worsening another.

The analysis focuses on linear multi-task models. In the under-parameterized setting, the authors identify a feasible region with multiple surfaces and establish necessary and sufficient conditions for full exploration of the Pareto front. Their results show that scalarization generally cannot reach the entire front, particularly balanced trade-offs among tasks.

Experiments on a real-world dataset compare scalarization with specialized multi-task optimizers. They corroborate the theoretical findings and show the potential of those optimizers to find balanced solutions inaccessible to scalarization. The contribution gives a geometric explanation for the shortfall beyond a general appeal to nonconvexity, while grounding its theoretical conclusions in the linear-model setting studied.
neurips-2023-revisiting-scalarization-in.tldr: For the studied linear multi-task models, weighted loss sums generally miss parts of the Pareto front, including balanced trade-offs.

paragraphs: Separating leaves from wood in forest LiDAR scans supports measurement of leaf area, an important source of uncertainty in vegetation-atmosphere gas-exchange models. Drones make repeated observation practical, but their small sensors produce relatively sparse point clouds. Occlusion also reduces sampling density deeper in the canopy, making the data spatially uneven.

The paper introduces a PointNet++-based neural network that uses point geometry without spectral information. Its sampling scheme aims to preserve locally important geometric details when nearby measurements are scarce. A specially adapted loss function addresses the severe imbalance between the classes, tackling a separate source of difficulty in learning leaf-versus-wood distinctions.

The model outperforms existing state-of-the-art alternatives on UAV point clouds. The findings support adapting both sampling and the training objective to the particular structure of sparse canopy measurements. The authors also discuss possible future improvements for much denser scans collected from below the canopy, distinguishing that prospect from the demonstrated results on aerial data.
neurips-2023-semantic-segmentation-of-sp.tldr: Geometry-preserving sampling and an imbalance-aware loss improve leaf-versus-wood segmentation in sparse, uneven UAV LiDAR scans.

paragraphs: Sketching compresses information so algorithms can use less memory or compute approximations efficiently. This paper develops sketching techniques for sparse dictionary learning and Euclidean k-means, emphasizing the requirement to output an assignment for every input point. That output requirement is central to the memory questions it studies.

The authors obtain a new route to polynomial-time approximation schemes for k-means and extend it to the first such scheme for sparse dictionary learning. They also analyze turnstile streams, where matrix entries receive updates. Ignoring logarithmic factors, the space upper bounds are nr/epsilon² + dk/epsilon for an r-sparse dictionary of size k, and n/epsilon² + dk/epsilon for k-means on n points with d dimensions.

For randomly ordered row insertions, k-means needs roughly linear space in n under a bounded-sensitivity assumption. Lower bounds establish unavoidable memory requirements, including a stronger requirement for algorithms estimating the cost of a fixed candidate center set. Together, these results characterize both achievable compression and limits on streaming solutions.
neurips-2023-sketching-algorithms-for-sp.tldr: New sketching techniques yield approximation schemes and streaming memory bounds for sparse dictionary learning and k-means with per-point outputs.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a two-dimensional floorplan from an unstructured three-dimensional point cloud requires more than recovering an approximate outline. Room shapes must be plausible, the representation must remain manageable, and local geometry must be captured accurately. SLIBO-Net addresses these three aspects together.

The method uses a transformer architecture with a slicing-box floorplan representation. The representation improves room-shape supervision while keeping the number of tokens manageable. Geometric priors enter both as regularization during learning and through post-processing, helping the system recover local details that matter to the quality of the reconstructed plan.

The authors also introduce a scale-independent evaluation metric to address unequal treatment of errors across floorplans of different sizes. On Structure3D, SLIBO-Net achieves a new state-of-the-art result, with reconstructions described as more semantically plausible and realistic. The contribution combines representation, geometric guidance, and evaluation design to improve how floorplans are produced and how their reconstruction quality is assessed.
neurips-2023-slibo-net-floorplan-reconst.tldr: SLIBO-Net combines an efficient floorplan representation with geometric guidance to improve reconstruction quality from 3D point clouds.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether synthetic images can train strong visual representations. Using Stable Diffusion, the authors find that self-supervised learning on generated images can match or exceed learning on corresponding real images when the generator is configured appropriately. The result makes generator configuration part of the conditions behind the comparison.

StableRep builds on the fact that one text prompt can produce several different images. It treats those images as positive examples for one another in a multi-positive contrastive objective. This encourages the representation to connect visually different outputs that share the same textual source.

On large-scale datasets, StableRep representations learned solely from synthetic images outperform SimCLR and CLIP representations trained using the same prompts and corresponding real images. Adding language supervision produces another favorable comparison: 20 million synthetic images from 10 million captions outperform CLIP trained on 50 million real images and captions. These findings establish strong empirical potential for generated training imagery under the studied configurations.
neurips-2023-stablerep-synthetic-images-.tldr: StableRep learns strong visual representations by treating multiple synthetic images generated from the same prompt as contrastive positives.

paragraphs: Diffusion models demand substantial storage and computation because they are large and generate outputs through repeated steps. Quantization reduces numerical precision to make models more economical. However, existing methods struggle to preserve diffusion-model quality even at eight-bit precision because activation values change over the course of generation.

The proposed method makes the quantization interval depend on the generation timestep. This lets the numerical range used for quantization follow temporal changes in the model’s activations. The timestep supplies the information needed to adapt the interval, directly addressing the variation that causes difficulty for existing quantization techniques.

The authors report that this adaptation adds no inference computation overhead and works with both post-training quantization and quantization-aware training. Experiments across multiple configurations show substantial improvements in output quality for quantized models. The contribution is a diffusion-specific adjustment to quantization that preserves more generation quality while remaining compatible with two established ways of preparing low-precision networks.
neurips-2023-temporal-dynamic-quantizati.tldr: Timestep-dependent quantization intervals improve diffusion-model output quality without adding inference computation overhead.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can produce combinatorial optimization policies without requiring expert-designed solutions or pre-solved training instances. Yet difficult optimization problems often need more than a single attempt at inference. This paper proposes learning a population of complementary policies whose solutions can be generated simultaneously.

The training procedure, Poppy, encourages specialization through the performance of the population as a whole. It does not require a manually specified definition of diversity. The motivation is that policies should differ in ways that improve collective solution quality, allowing different members to contribute useful behavior across the problems they encounter.

Experiments show that Poppy learns complementary policies and achieves state-of-the-art reinforcement-learning results on traveling salesman, capacitated vehicle routing, and job-shop scheduling problems. These findings support population training as an effective way to prepare multiple solution attempts for inference. The reported advances concern reinforcement-learning approaches on those three NP-hard problem families, where coordinated specialization provides a useful alternative source of solution diversity.
neurips-2023-winner-takes-it-all-trainin.tldr: Poppy trains complementary policy populations through collective performance, achieving leading reinforcement-learning results on three combinatorial optimization problems.
